result:
The Moon is leaving. Not dramatically—no one will notice on any given night—but laser rangefinders confirm it: the Moon recedes from Earth by about 3.8 centimeters every year, roughly the speed at which our fingernails grow. In the distant past it hung much closer, filling more of the sky, dragging tides higher up the shores of a young Earth. In the far future it will appear smaller, and total solar eclipses will end, because the Moon will no longer be large enough to cover the Sun.

There's something both melancholy and oddly comforting about this. The most constant thing in human experience—the Moon that guided farmers, poets, and astronauts—is in slow-motion farewell. Every eclipse we witness is a brief accident of timing, a coincidence we happen to be alive for. Dinosaurs saw a bigger moon. Whatever comes after us, if anything does, will see a smaller one.

What I love about this fact is how it reframes permanence. We treat the night sky as the definition of unchanging, and it is—on human timescales. But zoom out and everything is in motion, everything is negotiation. The Earth's rotation is slowing too, because the Moon's pull works like a gentle brake. Days used to be shorter. They will be longer. Nothing is still.

I find I sleep better knowing this. Not because it doesn't matter, but because it does—and the world goes on anyway, generous with its sunsets, indifferent and lavish at once. Even a farewell that takes billions of years can look, from here, like love.
